title: What is database sharding, what are its types (horizontal/vertical/geographic/hash), and its advantages and disadvantages?
shortTitle: What is database sharding, what are its types, and its advantages and disadvantages

s1_definition.profdef: Database sharding is horizontally partitioning a dataset across multiple independent database nodes, called shards, so that each shard holds only a subset of the rows and no single node holds the whole dataset. This spreads storage, memory, and write-and-read load across machines, enabling scale beyond what one node can handle. Common partitioning schemes include range-based, hash-based, directory or lookup-based, and geographic sharding, and the distinction from vertical partitioning is that sharding splits rows across nodes whereas vertical partitioning splits columns or tables. Its advantages are near-linear horizontal scale and fault isolation, and its disadvantages are operational complexity, expensive cross-shard queries and transactions, and the difficulty of rebalancing.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has so many customers that one giant ledger book is too heavy to lift and too slow to search. So the bank splits customers across many ledger books, maybe A to M in one book and N to Z in another, so each book is lighter and faster. A clerk only needs to open one book to find a given customer. The trade is that answering "how many customers do we have in total" now means adding up every book, and moving money between two customers in different books is harder because two books must be updated together.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sharding splits rows across many independent database nodes by a shard key so no node holds everything, giving horizontal scale and fault isolation at the cost of cross-shard complexity and hard rebalancing.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Database sharding is horizontally partitioning a dataset across multiple independent database nodes, called shards, so that each shard holds only a subset of the rows and no single node holds the whole dataset. This spreads storage, memory, and write-and-read load across machines, enabling scale beyond what one node can handle. Common partitioning schemes include range-based, hash-based, directory or lookup-based, and geographic sharding, and the distinction from vertical partitioning is that sharding splits rows across nodes whereas vertical partitioning splits columns or tables. Its advantages are near-linear horizontal scale and fault isolation, and its disadvantages are operational complexity, expensive cross-shard queries and transactions, and the difficulty of rebalancing.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has so many customers that one giant ledger book is too heavy to lift and too slow to search. So the bank splits customers across many ledger books, maybe A to M in one book and N to Z in another, so each book is lighter and faster. A clerk only needs to open one book to find a given customer. The trade is that answering "how many customers do we have in total" now means adding up every book, and moving money between two customers in different books is harder because two books must be updated together.

**One line to remember:** Sharding splits rows across many independent database nodes by a shard key so no node holds everything, giving horizontal scale and fault isolation at the cost of cross-shard complexity and hard rebalancing.

sections.s2_technical:
The motivation for sharding is that a single database node has hard limits: finite disk, memory, CPU, and connection capacity, and even with a powerful machine and read replicas you eventually cannot store or write enough on one node. Replication, as in master-slave, scales reads but not writes, because every write still goes to one master. Sharding is the technique that scales writes and total data size by distributing the rows themselves across many nodes, each of which is a fully independent database handling its own slice, so the aggregate capacity grows as you add shards.

The central concept is the shard key, the column whose value decides which shard a row lives on. Choosing it well is the most important decision in sharding, because it determines both how evenly data and load spread and how efficiently queries run, and a poor choice causes hot spots and expensive cross-shard operations. The partitioning scheme is the rule that maps a shard key to a shard.

Range-based sharding assigns contiguous ranges of the key to shards, for example accounts with ids one to one million on shard one, one million to two million on shard two. Its strength is that range queries, like "all accounts in this id band", hit a single shard, and adding a new range for new data is easy. Its weakness is that it easily creates hot spots: if new accounts always have the highest ids, the newest shard receives all the write traffic while older shards go cold, and uneven key distribution skews load.

Hash-based sharding applies a hash function to the key and uses the result, typically modulo the number of shards, to pick a shard, for example shard equals hash of account id modulo N. Its strength is excellent even distribution, since a good hash scatters keys uniformly, avoiding the hot spots that plague range sharding. Its weakness is that it destroys locality, so range queries now scatter across all shards, and the naive modulo form makes rebalancing painful because changing the number of shards remaps almost every key, which is why consistent hashing is used instead for systems that grow.

Directory or lookup-based sharding keeps an explicit mapping, a lookup table, from key or key-range to shard, so the routing is data rather than a formula. Its strength is maximum flexibility: you can place any key on any shard and move keys around by updating the table, which makes rebalancing and custom placement easy. Its weakness is that the lookup table is an extra dependency on every request and a potential single point of failure and bottleneck, so it must itself be highly available and cached.

Geographic sharding partitions by location, placing each region's data on shards in or near that region, for example Indian customers on shards in India and European customers on shards in Europe. Its strengths are low latency because data is near users, and data-residency compliance because regulations often require citizens' data to stay in-country, which is very relevant to banking. Its weakness is that cross-region operations are slow and complex, and load can be uneven if one region is far busier than another.

It is important to distinguish sharding, which is horizontal partitioning splitting rows across nodes, from vertical partitioning, which splits a table's columns or splits different tables onto different nodes, such as putting the rarely-read profile columns on one node and hot transactional columns on another. They solve different problems and are sometimes combined.

The advantages are clear. Horizontal scalability lets you handle more data and more writes by adding shards, roughly linearly. Fault isolation means a single shard's failure affects only the customers on that shard, not everyone. Smaller per-shard datasets mean smaller indexes and faster queries on each node, and you can place shards for locality.

The disadvantages are equally important and are where senior judgement shows. Operational complexity rises sharply: you run and monitor many databases, route every query to the right shard, and handle shard failures individually. Cross-shard queries are expensive, because a query that needs data from every shard becomes a scatter-gather that fans out to all shards and merges results, which is slow and hard. Cross-shard transactions lose single-node ACID guarantees, so a transfer between two accounts on different shards needs a distributed transaction or a saga, which is complex and can leave intermediate states. Rebalancing is hard, because adding or removing shards can require moving large amounts of data, especially with naive hashing. And joins across shards are impractical, so schemas are often denormalized and related data co-located to keep common operations on a single shard.

Senior nuances: shard only when you must, because the complexity is real and a single well-tuned node with replicas handles more than people expect; choose a shard key that both spreads load evenly and keeps your most common queries on one shard; co-locate related data, for example all of a customer's accounts and transactions on the same shard; and prefer consistent hashing over modulo so growth does not trigger a massive remap.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's single database could no longer store or write the volume of customer accounts and transactions, and adding read replicas did not help the write bottleneck. This is exactly the horizontal-scaling case sharding solves, splitting accounts across many shards so writes spread out.

Problem 2 — The team debated how to map accounts to shards, and saw that range by id put all new accounts on one hot shard, while hashing spread them evenly but scattered range queries. This is exactly the comparison of range versus hash sharding and their trade-offs.

Problem 3 — Regulators required that Indian customers' data stay in India. This is exactly geographic sharding, placing data by region for residency compliance and latency.

Our mini-project demonstrates the schemes. The code defines an `Account`, a `ShardRouter` that can route by range, by hash, or by region, a set of in-memory `Shard` nodes, and a demo that inserts accounts under each scheme and shows the distribution, highlighting the hot-shard problem of range sharding, the even spread of hashing, and the regional placement of geographic sharding, plus a scatter-gather count across all shards.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: twelve accounts with increasing ids and a mix of Indian and European regions, inserted under each sharding strategy across four shards.

Step 1: Under hash sharding, each account's id is hashed and taken modulo four to pick a shard. Because a good hash scatters values, the accounts land roughly evenly across all four shards, which is the strength of hashing, no hot shard.

Step 2: Under range sharding, accounts are placed by contiguous id ranges, so the lowest ids go to shard zero and the highest to shard three. Since ids increase over time, the newest accounts all pile onto the last range, creating a hot shard that would absorb most new writes while earlier shards go cold.

Step 3: Under geographic sharding, each account is routed by its region, so Indian accounts go to the India shards and European accounts to the Europe shards. This keeps data near its users and satisfies residency rules, though if one region has far more customers that region's shards carry more load.

Step 4: For each strategy the demo prints the per-shard counts, making the distribution visible: even for hash, skewed toward the last shard for range, and region-aligned for geographic.

Step 5: To answer a global question like the total account count, the router performs a scatter-gather, querying every shard and summing the results, which always returns twelve but illustrates that cross-shard aggregates must touch all shards and are therefore expensive at scale. The output shows the three distributions and the scatter-gather totals.

```
2026-10-24 15:18:55 INFO    HASH distribution: shard0(IN)=3 shard1(IN)=3 shard2(EU)=3 shard3(EU)=3
2026-10-24 15:18:55 INFO    HASH scatter-gather total accounts = 12
2026-10-24 15:18:55 INFO    RANGE distribution: shard0(IN)=4 shard1(IN)=4 shard2(EU)=4 shard3(EU)=0
2026-10-24 15:18:55 INFO    RANGE scatter-gather total accounts = 12
2026-10-24 15:18:55 INFO    GEOGRAPHIC distribution: shard0(IN)=8 shard1(IN)=0 shard2(EU)=4 shard3(EU)=0
2026-10-24 15:18:55 INFO    GEOGRAPHIC scatter-gather total accounts = 12
```

```
  ═══ LLD — Sharding Schemes (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Strategy: RANGE / HASH / GEOGRAPHIC / DIRECTORY routing       │
  │   WHY: swap partitioning scheme without changing callers      │
  │ Router/Proxy: ShardRouter maps key → shard                   │
  │   WHY: callers stay oblivious to physical placement           │
  │ Scatter-Gather: fan out to all shards + merge                 │
  │   WHY: answer global queries across partitions                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: ShardRouter routes; Shard stores; Account is data          │
  │ O: new scheme = new strategy branch, no caller change         │
  │ L: any strategy returns a valid Shard                         │
  │ D: services depend on ShardRouter, not shard nodes            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────┐ routes ┌──────────┐ stores ┌──────────┐
  │ ShardRouter   │───────▶│ Shard     │───────▶│ Account   │
  │ +shardFor()   │        │ +insert() │        │ id,bal,   │
  │ +scatterGather│        │ +count()  │        │ region    │
  └──────────────┘        └──────────┘        └──────────┘

  ── Decision: which scheme? ────────────────────────────────────
  Range queries on key common?   → RANGE (watch hot shards)
  Need even load, point lookups?  → HASH (consistent hashing for growth)
  Data residency / locality?       → GEOGRAPHIC
  Need arbitrary placement/moves?  → DIRECTORY (HA lookup table)
  Split columns, not rows?          → vertical partitioning (different problem)

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. shardFor(account) → pick shard by strategy
  2. shard.insert(account) → single-node write
  3. point read → one shard (cheap)
  4. global count → scatterGatherCount() → all shards + sum (expensive)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Database sharding is horizontally partitioning a dataset across multiple independent database nodes, called shards, so each shard holds only a subset of the rows and no single node holds everything. I reach for it because a single node has hard limits on disk, memory, CPU, and connections, and while replication like master-slave scales reads, it does not scale writes because every write still goes to one master. Sharding scales writes and total data size by distributing the rows themselves, so aggregate capacity grows as I add shards. The most important decision is the shard key, the column that decides which shard a row lives on, because it governs how evenly data and load spread and how efficiently queries run.

There are several partitioning schemes. Range-based assigns contiguous key ranges to shards, which makes range queries hit one shard but easily creates hot spots when new data always lands at one end. Hash-based applies a hash and typically takes it modulo the shard count, giving excellent even distribution but destroying locality so range queries scatter, and the naive modulo form makes rebalancing painful, which is why consistent hashing is preferred for systems that grow. Directory or lookup-based keeps an explicit mapping table from key to shard, giving maximum flexibility and easy rebalancing at the cost of an extra highly-available dependency on every request. Geographic sharding partitions by location, placing each region's data near its users, which gives low latency and satisfies data-residency rules that are very relevant in banking, but makes cross-region operations slow. I always distinguish this horizontal row-splitting from vertical partitioning, which splits columns or tables across nodes and solves a different problem.

The advantages are horizontal write scalability roughly linear in the number of shards, fault isolation so one shard's failure affects only its customers, and smaller per-shard datasets with smaller, faster indexes. The disadvantages are where judgement matters: operational complexity rises sharply because I run and monitor many databases and route every query; cross-shard queries become expensive scatter-gather operations that fan out to all shards and merge; cross-shard transactions lose single-node ACID so a transfer between accounts on different shards needs a distributed transaction or a saga; rebalancing is hard because adding shards can require moving huge amounts of data; and joins across shards are impractical, so I denormalize and co-locate related data.

On my project at National Bank of India our single database could no longer handle the write volume even with replicas, so we sharded accounts, and we saw the trade-offs directly: ranging by id put all new accounts on one hot shard, hashing spread them evenly but scattered range queries, and we used geographic sharding to keep Indian customers' data in India for compliance. The lessons I always give are to shard only when a single well-tuned node with replicas truly cannot cope because the complexity is real, to choose a shard key that both spreads load evenly and keeps common queries on one shard, to co-locate related data like all of a customer's accounts and transactions on the same shard, and to prefer consistent hashing over modulo so growth does not trigger a massive remap.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that sharding splits rows across many independent nodes by a shard key, using range, hash, directory, or geographic schemes, giving horizontal write scale and fault isolation but costing operational complexity, expensive scatter-gather queries, hard cross-shard transactions, and painful rebalancing, so I shard only when I must and choose the key to keep common queries on one shard.

keyPoints: Database per service: each microservice owns its data
Idempotency: same request produces same result — safe retries
Eventual consistency: services sync via events, not distributed locks
Shared database anti-pattern: breaks service independence
